opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's going to be uneven. "AI for Science" isn't one market, it's a dozen different ones moving on very different clocks.

The fastest movers are areas where the AI output plugs directly into an existing workflow and someone already has a budget for it. Protein structure prediction, molecular property prediction, materials screening, and simulation acceleration in engineering are good examples. If a chemist or a structural biologist can use a model to cut a month of computation or wet-lab screening down to a few days, they'll pay for that today. Those businesses are already generating real revenue, mostly as tools and platforms sold to pharma, chemicals, semiconductors and energy companies.

The slower part, and the part that gets the headlines, is the promise of "AI discovered a drug" or "AI discovered a new material" that actually reaches the market. That's bottlenecked by the physical world: clinical trials, synthesis, scale-up, manufacturing, regulation. AI can compress the front end of drug discovery, maybe taking you from target to candidate in a year and a half instead of four or five. But a Phase III trial still takes as long as it takes. So realistically, the first wave of clearly AI-originated drugs reaching approval is a story for the next several years, and whether they actually succeed at higher rates than traditional pipelines is still an open question. That's the number the industry really needs to prove.

I'd also say the biggest constraint right now isn't the models, it's data. In language and vision you had the internet. In science, high-quality, standardized experimental data is scarce, expensive and siloed inside companies. So I think the winners commercially will be the teams that close the loop by pairing models with automated labs, generating their own proprietary data, and getting better with every iteration. That "lab-in-the-loop" model is where I see a lot of the durable value forming over the next three to five years.

So my rough framing is this. Tools and infrastructure are commercializing now. Platform partnerships with big industry players are scaling over the next few years. Truly AI-native products like drugs, materials and chemicals proving out at scale are more of a five-to-ten-year horizon. People who expect the ChatGPT-style overnight curve here will be disappointed. People who are patient and focused on the data and the experimental loop are building something very big.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can shorten drug discovery from target to candidate and that tools and platforms already earn revenue, while AI-originated drugs reaching approval remain years away.

r002.rationale: It discusses scientific commercialization and data bottlenecks, but does not say Nobel-level results require advancing AI’s capabilities.

r003.rationale: Science is presented as an application area for AI; the response does not describe science as a catalyst for improving AI itself.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim that models solving difficult scientific problems should outperform current models on problems outside science.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing, because "AI for Science" isn't one thing with one timeline. It's a stack of very different problems, and they commercialize at very different speeds.

The fastest layer is where the science already has a well-defined, measurable target and lots of existing data. Protein structure, small-molecule screening, some materials property prediction. There you're really just replacing an expensive physical step with a cheaper computational step, and the economics are obvious. That's commercializing now. Pharma is paying for it today, even if the drugs that come out the other end are still five or ten years from approval.

The middle layer is harder. That's things like inverse design: tell me a material with this bandgap and this stability, and give me something I can actually synthesize. Prediction is easy. Synthesizability is the wall. I spent years in a lab stacking two-dimensional materials by hand, and the gap between "this structure should exist" and "I can make it on a Tuesday afternoon" is enormous. Closing that gap means automating the lab itself, and that's robotics, instrumentation, and a lot of unglamorous engineering. I think that's a five to ten year horizon before it's a real business at scale.

And then the deepest layer is AI actually doing discovery, generating a hypothesis nobody had, and that's where I'd be most cautious. The honest answer is we don't know. The models are getting impressive at reading and summarizing the literature, but discovery is usually about noticing the anomaly everyone else ignored. Magic-angle graphene came out of a measurement that looked like a mistake at first. I don't think we've shown AI can do that yet.

So if you ask me for a single number, I'd say: real revenue now in a few narrow verticals, broad industrial adoption toward the end of this decade, and the genuinely transformative version is an open scientific question, not a product roadmap. I'd be suspicious of anyone who gives you a cleaner answer than that.

r001.rationale: The response says pharma is paying for computational steps now while resulting drugs remain years from approval, communicating that intermediate products can be commercialized first.

r002.rationale: It says AI discovery has not yet been demonstrated, but does not state that Nobel-level results require advancing AI capabilities.

r003.rationale: The response does not frame science as a catalyst for improving AI itself.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim that models solving difficult scientific problems would also outperform current models on non-scientific problems.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate two things: when AI becomes useful in scientific work, and when that usefulness turns into a sustainable business. Those timelines can be quite different.

For tools that help researchers analyze data, write code, or screen candidates, the path to commercialization can be relatively short. You can fit into an existing workflow and show that you save time or reduce costs. But if you’re using AI to develop a new drug or a new material, a better prediction is only one step. You still need experiments, validation, and eventually manufacturing or clinical trials. AI can accelerate parts of that process, but it doesn’t eliminate the whole cycle.

So I’d expect commercialization to happen in waves. The earlier opportunities are likely to be narrowly defined problems where the customer can measure the value. The bigger scientific outcomes will take longer, and their timing will depend heavily on the field.

For me, the key question is whether you can close the loop between a model’s prediction and experimental results. If you can do that reliably, and at a cost customers are willing to pay, you have the basis for a business.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes near-term research tools from longer drug-development outcomes, but does not say that intermediate products of AI-assisted drug development can be sold before a finished AI-generated drug.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Nobel-level results or say that reaching them requires advancing AI capabilities.

r003.rationale: It discusses AI helping scientific work, but does not frame science as a catalyst for improving AI itself.

r004.rationale: It makes no claim that models solving difficult scientific problems would also outperform current models on non-scientific problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think commercialization will happen at different speeds across different fields. The key question is whether AI can solve a valuable problem and whether that improvement can be verified in the real world.

In the near term, the clearest opportunities are tools that help scientists work faster—analyzing data, running simulations, or choosing which experiments to do next. Those can create value within existing research workflows. But discovering a new material or developing a drug takes longer, because a model’s prediction is only one step. You still need experiments, manufacturing, and, in some cases, regulatory approval.

So I would distinguish between commercializing a research tool and commercializing the scientific discovery itself. The first can happen relatively quickly; the second depends on the development cycle of the industry. I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t put all of AI for Science on a single timeline.

r001.rationale: It says research tools can be commercialized faster than scientific discoveries, but does not clearly identify intermediate products of AI-assisted drug development as commercializable before a finished AI-generated drug.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Nobel-level results or the need to advance AI capabilities to achieve them.

r003.rationale: It does not frame science as a catalyst for improving AI itself.

r004.rationale: It does not state that models solving difficult scientific problems should also outperform current models on non-scientific problems.
